What to look for. The confidence interval captures uncertainty about the mean effect at the specified best-practice covariate values, holding the model fixed. The prediction interval is wider because it also incorporates the residual effect heterogeneity: even among studies that match the best-practice profile, effects will vary due to factors not captured by the model. If the prediction interval is very wide relative to the confidence interval, substantial unexplained heterogeneity remains and the best-practice estimate should be interpreted cautiously as a central tendency rather than a precise forecast.

It is also worth comparing the size of these best-practice estimates to the CHE PET intercept in Panel B of Table 5 (0.042 in Fisher’s z), which nets out the same publication-bias correction but evaluates the 18 study-characteristic moderators at their sample averages rather than at best-practice values. The best-practice predictions (-0.022 for non-OECD/Europe, -0.043 for OECD/Europe) are, like this benchmark, small in magnitude and statistically indistinguishable from zero. The shift induced by centering the meta-regression at an idealized set of covariate values is not trivial (for the OECD/Europe scenario it modestly exceeds the Doucouliagos (2011) small-effect threshold), but it is smaller than the shift induced by the publication-bias correction itself, and it leaves the estimate in the same place: near zero. This suggests that, in this literature, publication-bias correction – not adjustment for study design and methodology – is doing most of the work in bringing the raw, uncorrected CHE mean (0.175, Table 4) down toward zero.

9 Further Analysis: Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis

The analysis in Sections 6 through 8 rests on a specific approach to publication bias: the FAT-PET regression, which tests for a linear association between effect size and standard error and corrects for it by setting the standard error to zero. This approach is well established and widely used (Wu et al., 2026), but it embeds a particular assumption about the selection process that may not hold in all literatures. Specifically, FAT-PET assumes that the probability of publication is a monotone function of the ratio of the effect size to its standard error, so that the standard error is a sufficient proxy for the degree of selection. When this assumption fails – for example, when selection operates on the sign of the effect rather than only its significance, or when the relationship between effect size and standard error is nonlinear – FAT-PET may provide a distorted correction. This is not merely a hypothetical concern: Section 6’s robustness checks found strong evidence of selection specifically against wrong-signed results (\(\hat{\lambda}_2 = 0.27\), with a bootstrap confidence interval excluding 1) that PET-PEESE’s smooth, standard-error-only form cannot represent.

Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA; Bartoš et al., 2023) addresses this limitation by combining multiple models of the selection process within a Bayesian model-averaging framework. Rather than committing to a single correction method, RoBMA assigns prior probabilities to a set of competing models that include both regression-based adjustments analogous to PET and PEESE and step-function selection models analogous to the 3PSM and 4PSM described in Section 6’s robustness checks. The posterior distribution over these models, updated by the data, determines which correction method receives the most weight in the final estimate. The result is a bias-corrected mean effect that is robust to uncertainty about the selection mechanism.

This section extends the protocol to include a RoBMA analysis. The primary aim is to assess whether the CHE-PET-PEESE corrected estimate from Table 5 Panel B and the RoBMA corrected estimate tell the same substantive story. If they agree, the FAT-PET result is corroborated by a more flexible approach and the conclusions of the preceding sections stand on firmer ground. If they diverge, RoBMA analysis can provide a credible alternative basis for drawing conclusions about the true underlying effect, and the divergence itself is a finding worth reporting.

9.1 What This Section Covers

The RoBMA analysis proceeds in five steps. The first fits an intercept-only multilevel RoBMA model and produces a z-plot (Figure 3), which displays the empirical distribution of z-statistics alongside the model-implied distribution and makes the nature and extent of publication bias directly visible. The second constructs a three-way comparison table (Table 8) that places the uncorrected CHE mean, the FAT-PET corrected mean, and the RoBMA bias-corrected mean side by side, together with Bayes factors for the three model components. The third uses BIC-based moderator pre-selection (Table 9) to identify which study characteristics should be included in the RoBMA meta-regression. The fourth fits the multilevel RoBMA meta-regression (Table 10), estimating publication-bias-corrected moderator effects and model-averaged regression coefficients. The fifth derives best-practice effect size predictions (Table 11), which are compared directly to their counterparts in Table 7.

9.2 Software Setup

The RoBMA analysis requires the RoBMA package (Bartoš et al., 2023). This package must be installed before running any script in this section. This package also requires JAGS to be installed on your system (see Software Setup in the Introduction); JAGS is not installed by install.packages().

Code 
install.packages("RoBMA")
Code 
library(RoBMA)
library(readxl)

9.3 The Z-Plot

The starting point for the RoBMA analysis is a visual inspection of the z-statistic distribution. The z-plot plays the same role for the RoBMA analysis that the funnel plot (Figure 2) plays for the PET-PEESE analysis in Section 6: a visual, motivational diagnostic that precedes the formal estimates and suggests which selection mechanisms are at work. Each effect size in the database can be converted to a z-statistic by dividing it by its standard error. Under a model with no publication bias, the distribution of these z-statistics generally should be smooth and unimodal, reflecting the underlying distribution of true effects combined with sampling variability. When publication bias is present, the distribution is distorted: observations accumulate at thresholds that carry particular significance for the probability of publication.

The z-plot displays the empirical histogram of z-statistics alongside the model-averaged curve implied by the fitted RoBMA model. This curve is a fitted plot representing the family of selection models included in RoBMA, weighted by their posterior probabilities, and is shown with a pointwise 95% uncertainty band.

For this step, an intercept-only multilevel RoBMA model is fitted on the full dataset. The multilevel structure accounts for the dependence among effect sizes nested within studies, consistent with the CHE approach used throughout the preceding sections. The model is specified with measure = "ZCOR" because the input is Fisher’s z-transformed partial correlations, and with cluster = newid to define the study-level clustering. The fitted model object is saved as RoBMA_intercept_only.rds so that Table 8 can load it without refitting.

What about other effect sizes? This protocol illustrates RoBMA using Fisher’s z-transformed partial correlations, but measure accepts five other standardized effect-size types directly, with no additional setup required: standardized mean differences ("SMD"), risk ratios ("RR"), odds ratios ("OR"), hazard ratios ("HR"), and incidence rate ratios ("IRR"). Each of these, like "ZCOR", has a known unit information standard deviation built into RoBMA, which is what lets the package scale its default priors automatically without any further input from the researcher. A nonstandard effect size without a known unit information standard deviation, a raw regression coefficient being the most common example, requires a different procedure, using measure = "GEN" together with either sample sizes or a manually supplied scaling factor. This case is discussed in detail in a comment in Protocol_Figure3.R, the first script in this protocol to fit a RoBMA model.

A note on MCMC convergence. Before interpreting output from this or any subsequent RoBMA model, the researcher should confirm that the MCMC chains have converged. RoBMA applies automatic convergence checks to every fitted model, by default requiring an R-hat below 1.05 and an effective sample size of at least 500, and prints a warning whenever a model fails them. These warnings should not be ignored. Estimates from models showing convergence problems should be interpreted with caution, although the seriousness of the problem depends on the parameter and diagnostic involved. If a warning appears, the remedy is to increase the sampling effort (the sample, burnin, and adapt settings) or to refit with autofit = TRUE, which extends the chains automatically until the convergence criteria are met, rather than to interpret the estimates as they stand. Visual checks are also available through plot_diagnostic(), which produces trace, autocorrelation, and density plots for individual parameters. A worked example, showing these diagnostics for the meta-regression in Table 10, appears directly below that table.

9.3.1 Run the script

Code 
# Note: this script takes approximately 5 hours to run on the full dataset.
# The fitted model is saved as RoBMA_intercept_only.rds for use in Table 8.
source("Protocol_Figure3.R")

9.3.2 Display the output

Code 
knitr::include_graphics("Figure3_Zplot.png")

What to look for. The z-plot reveals publication bias through two distinct features of the empirical histogram that should be read against the smooth model curve. The first is a spike at z = 0, the boundary between positive and negative effect sizes. The accumulation of z-statistics just above zero reflects selection for the correct sign of the effect: studies showing a positive association between social capital and economic growth are more likely to be reported than studies showing a negative association, regardless of statistical significance.

The second is a spike at z ≈ 1.96, the conventional threshold for two-sided statistical significance at the five percent level. The sharp changes in the histogram at the directional and statistical-significance thresholds indicate strong selective reporting. The fitted RoBMA curve highlights these discontinuities, although it does not fully capture their magnitude.

The model-averaged curve is the fit of RoBMA’s candidate models, weighted by their posterior probabilities, to the observed histogram. The bias-corrected mean effect is obtained separately, from the model-averaged parameter estimates reported in Table 8.

The z-plot above echoes the PML step-function findings from Section 6’s robustness checks: \(\hat{\lambda}_2 = 0.27\), with a confidence interval excluding 1, showed strong selection against wrong-signed results, consistent with the near-absence of negative z-statistics here, while \(\hat{\lambda}_1\), estimated at 0.75 to 0.79 with a confidence interval including 1, showed only weak selection against positive-but-insignificant results, consistent with their visible accumulation just above zero.

That two different estimation approaches, one a smooth Bayesian model average, the other explicit p-value thresholds, converge on the same qualitative pattern is independent evidence that selection in this literature operates on sign, not just significance.

9.4 Comparing Publication Bias Corrections

Table 8 places the RoBMA bias-corrected mean alongside the two estimates from the preceding sections: the uncorrected CHE mean from Table 4 and the FAT-PET corrected mean from Table 5. The purpose is to determine whether RoBMA and FAT-PET are telling the same substantive story at the pooled level. If the two corrected estimates agree, RoBMA is not adding new information about the pooled mean; if they diverge, the source and implications of the divergence must be examined further. This pooled comparison is only the first step: the moderator-adjusted analysis in Tables 9 through 11 addresses a distinct question and is carried out regardless, since agreement about the pooled mean does not guarantee agreement once study characteristics are taken into account.

The FAT-PET corrected estimate used in this comparison is the PET intercept from the CHE model in Table 5 Panel B. In the analysis of this dataset, no intercept in Table 5 Panel B reached conventional statistical significance, so the PEESE sensitivity analysis (Table 5S) was not triggered and the PET intercept is the appropriate reference point for the publication bias correction.

Table 8 also reports, in a second panel, the inclusion Bayes factors for the three model components estimated by the intercept-only RoBMA: the effect component (whether the mean effect is nonzero), the heterogeneity component (whether there is genuine between-study variability), and the publication bias component (whether selective reporting is present). These Bayes factors quantify the evidence in favor of each component and require no additional estimation beyond the model already fitted for Figure 3.

9.4.1 Run the script

Code 
source("Protocol_Table8.R")

9.4.2 Display the output

Code 
read_excel("Table8_RoBMA_Comparison.xlsx", sheet = "Comparison") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Panel A: Mean effect estimates across correction methods (Fisher's z scale)", digits = 3)
read_excel("Table8_RoBMA_Comparison.xlsx", sheet = "BayesFactors") |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Panel B: RoBMA component inclusion Bayes factors", digits = 3)

What to look for. In Panel A, the key comparison is between the FAT-PET corrected mean and the RoBMA corrected mean. If these two estimates are close in magnitude, the pooled conclusions of the preceding sections are robust to the choice of correction method; if they diverge substantially, the divergence is itself a finding worth examining. In this dataset, the two methods diverge substantially. FAT-PET reduces the raw CHE mean of 0.175 by roughly 76 percent, to 0.042, an estimate whose confidence interval comfortably includes zero (Table 5). RoBMA’s intercept-only model reduces the same raw mean by only about 31 percent, to 0.121, with a 95% credible interval of [0.073, 0.170] that excludes zero entirely. At the pooled level, then, FAT-PET’s linear correction removes essentially all of the raw association, while RoBMA’s model-averaged correction leaves an effect that remains credibly different from zero – a first indication that the two frameworks are not simply reweighted versions of the same conclusion. The gap between the two corrected means, roughly 0.08 in Fisher’s z, itself exceeds the Doucouliagos (2011) small-effect benchmark used elsewhere in this protocol.

In Panel B, the inclusion Bayes factors characterize the evidence for each model component. A Bayes factor above 100 is conventionally considered decisive evidence; here all three components – the presence of an overall effect, genuine between-study heterogeneity, and publication bias – reach RoBMA’s reporting ceiling of 59,999, with posterior inclusion probabilities of 1. The evidence for all three is about as strong as this method can register, which is itself informative: whatever the RoBMA-corrected mean turns out to be, the intercept-only model is unambiguous that there is a nonzero effect to correct, real between-study heterogeneity, and severe publication bias in this literature.

Decision point. Report Table 8 as a robustness check comparing the FAT-PET and RoBMA corrected means, and proceed to Table 9 regardless of whether they agree. Agreement at the pooled level would not have guaranteed that the moderator-level results in Table 10 also agree, and the disagreement found here does not preempt that separate analysis either.

9.5 Moderator Pre-Selection

Before fitting the RoBMA meta-regression, it is necessary to determine which of the 18 candidate moderators from Table 6 should be included in the model. The multilevel RoBMA meta-regression is substantially more computationally demanding than its CHE counterpart, and including all 18 moderators simultaneously would require prohibitive estimation time on standard hardware. A pre-selection step is therefore needed to reduce the moderator set to those variables most likely to contribute to the explanation of heterogeneity.

9.5.1 The BIC drop-one approach

The pre-selection strategy uses the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) applied to the CHE meta-regression from Table 6. BIC is chosen over less conservative criteria such as AIC for two reasons. Its heavier penalty on additional parameters suits the purpose of this step, which is to reduce the moderator set aggressively enough to make the RoBMA meta-regression computationally feasible. And BIC approximates the log marginal likelihood used in Bayesian model comparison, making it a natural screening criterion for a model that will itself be estimated in a Bayesian framework.

The full CHE model with all 18 moderators plus the standard error (sez) is estimated by maximum likelihood rather than restricted maximum likelihood, because BIC comparisons are only valid across models estimated on the same likelihood basis. When models differ in their fixed effects – as they do here, since each drop-one model omits a different moderator – REML log-likelihoods are not comparable and ML must be used instead. Each of the 18 moderators is then dropped from the model one at a time, and the change in BIC relative to the full model is recorded. A positive delta-BIC – meaning BIC increased when the variable was dropped – indicates that the variable improves fit and should be retained. A negative delta-BIC indicates that the variable can be excluded without penalty.

It is important to note that sez is included in the CHE models for this selection exercise but is not itself a candidate for dropping, and it will not be carried forward into the RoBMA meta-regression. The reason is that RoBMA corrects for publication bias internally through its model-averaging framework, which includes both regression-based and selection-model approaches. Adding sez as an explicit moderator in the RoBMA meta-regression would double-count the precision effect and conflate the publication bias correction with the substantive moderator analysis.

Moderators that cause convergence failures when dropped are treated as retained by default. If the model cannot be estimated without a particular variable, that variable is sufficiently entangled with the other regressors that its exclusion cannot be straightforwardly evaluated.

9.5.2 A note on the limitations of this approach

Readers should be aware that BIC-based pre-selection is a pragmatic compromise rather than the methodologically ideal approach to moderator selection within a RoBMA framework. A fully coherent Bayesian treatment would pass all candidate moderators to RoBMA simultaneously and allow the model’s own averaging mechanism to determine inclusion through posterior inclusion probabilities, exactly as RoBMA does for the publication bias correction. The pre-screening step introduced here is a form of pre-testing: the moderator inclusion probabilities and coefficients reported in Table 10 condition on the pre-selected model rather than averaging over the uncertainty about which moderators to include, which may overstate precision to some degree. Researchers with access to faster computing hardware or working with smaller datasets are encouraged to skip this step and run the full RoBMA meta-regression with all candidate moderators directly.

Code

source("Protocol_Table9.R")

Code 
tbl <- read_excel("Table9_BIC_ModeratorSelection.xlsx")

# The footnote is stored as its own row in the sheet, with a blank spacer

What to look for. The delta-BIC column is the key output. Variables with a positive delta-BIC are retained for the RoBMA meta-regression; those with a negative delta-BIC are excluded. Convergence failures are treated as retains and should be noted explicitly in reporting. The researcher should also consider whether any moderator excluded by BIC has a strong theoretical rationale that might justify its inclusion regardless of the BIC result. Note that one regional dummy, Reg_OECDEurope, will be added to the Table 10 model regardless of its BIC performance, since it is required for the best-practice predictions in Table 11 (see the Model specification subsection below for why only one of the four regional dummies is carried forward). In this dataset, only one of the 18 moderators, Endogeneity: FE (delta-BIC = 1.69), is retained; every other moderator shows a negative delta-BIC and is dropped, with no convergence failures in this run.

9.6 RoBMA Meta-Regression

Table 10 presents the multilevel RoBMA meta-regression. Its purpose is twofold: to estimate which study characteristics are genuinely associated with variation in effect sizes after correcting for publication bias, and to provide the model-averaged coefficients from which the best-practice predictions in Table 11 are derived.

This provides an alternative, arguably more credible, answer to the heterogeneity question than Table 6 because the CHE meta-regression in Table 6 corrects for publication bias through a single linear sez term. This implicitly assumes selective reporting operates uniformly across the sample, regardless of moderator values. If instead the severity of selective reporting depends on those same study characteristics, the sez term cannot capture that interaction. The resulting bias is then absorbed into the moderator coefficients themselves, contaminating the estimated moderator effects. RoBMA addresses this by estimating publication bias jointly with moderator effects, using a model-averaged combination of selection mechanisms rather than a single fixed linear form.

9.6.1 Model specification

Continuous moderators are standardized internally by RoBMA, making the prior distributions scale-invariant and centering the intercept on the grand mean effect. This means raw covariate values can be passed directly to the prediction step in Table 11 without manual standardization. The standard error (sez) is not included as a moderator, for the reasons described above.

Binary moderators are declared as factors rather than left as 0/1 integers, which matters in RoBMA specifically: a numeric predictor is treated as continuous and standardized, placing the continuous-predictor prior on the wrong scale for a binary indicator, whereas a factor receives the categorical-moderator prior. For the contrast coding of those factors this model uses treatment (dummy) coding, applied to every factor predictor via set_contrast_factor_predictors = "treatment". Under treatment coding the intercept is the estimate for the reference-level combination (Endog_FE = 0, Reg_OECDEurope = 0), and each factor’s coefficient is the difference associated with switching that indicator to 1 – the same interpretation the CHE coefficients in Table 6 already carry, so the two sets of coefficients can be compared directly in Panel C below.

The quantity comparable to the FAT-PET intercept in Panel B of Table 5 – the sample-weighted average effect across the moderators’ actual empirical distribution – is given by RoBMA’s pooled_effect() function, not by marginal_means(), which returns a different, unweighted average across a factor’s levels and is not the quantity Panel B’s estimate is meant to match.

One further point is worth stating. RoBMA’s inclusion Bayes factors compare models that include a given component to models that exclude it. Under treatment coding, the Effect component’s inclusion Bayes factor tests whether the reference-level intercept, the estimate for a study with Endog_FE = 0 and Reg_OECDEurope = 0, is distinguishable from zero. It is not a direct test of whether the pooled effect reported via pooled_effect() is distinguishable from zero, and the two need not agree. A moderator-free test of whether an overall effect exists at all is exactly what the intercept-only model in Table 8 already provides, and it remains the correctly scoped tool for that question regardless of what this model’s own Effect Bayes factor shows.

With these general modeling choices in place, the moderator actually retained from Table 9’s BIC pre-selection is Endogeneity: FE. One additional regional dummy, Reg_OECDEurope, is included regardless of its BIC performance, because it is required to construct the two best-practice scenarios in Table 11.

The model is fit using standard MCMC settings with parallel chains, and the fitted model object is saved as RoBMA_metaregression.rds for use in Table 11.

The current multilevel RoBMA framework does not allow for correlated effects, the “C” in CHE. It is instead based on a hierarchical-effects (HE) structure, which decomposes heterogeneity into between- and within-cluster components without assuming a correlation between multiple effect-size estimates drawn from the same study. Future releases of RoBMA are planned to add correlated-effects models directly in the Bayesian setting, which would allow a genuine CHE-style specification to be estimated within RoBMA’s model-averaging framework.

source("Protocol_Table10.R")

Every parameter is comfortably inside the R-hat < 1.05 / ESS ≥ 500 bar described in Section 9.3, so the estimates reported above can be interpreted with confidence. What to look for. Panel A shows that all three components are now decisive: heterogeneity, publication bias, and the Effect component itself each carry an inclusion Bayes factor exceeding 59,999 (posterior probability 1). Because the model uses treatment coding, the Effect component’s Bayes factor speaks specifically to the reference-level combination (Endog_FE = 0, Reg_OECDEurope = 0), not to the pooled effect directly (see Model specification above). The pooled, average-study bias-corrected mean, obtained separately via pooled_effect() and reported in Table 12, is 0.122, 95% CrI [0.073, 0.171]: small in size, but with an interval that excludes zero entirely. This is reassuringly close to the moderator-free, intercept-only estimate in Table 8 (0.121, CrI [0.073, 0.170]), exactly what should happen if conditioning on Endog_FE and Reg_OECDEurope is not distorting the average-study estimate. This model conditions on a narrower moderator set than earlier fits of this same meta-regression (see the Decision point below); what that means for the comparison with FAT-PET is taken up in Section 10. The substantive interpretation of the moderators themselves happens in the panels that follow.

Panel B reports the moderator inclusion probabilities. These are not directly comparable to the BMA posterior inclusion probabilities in Table 6: BMA is estimated by OLS, which ignores both inverse-variance weighting and the within-study dependence structure that this protocol is built around. RoBMA’s PIPs are estimated within a multilevel model that allows for hierarchical dependence within clusters, and that jointly corrects for publication bias rather than treating it as a separate linear term.

Panel C reports the model-averaged regression coefficients. Under treatment coding, the intercept (0.132, 95% CrI [0.081, 0.185]) is not a grand-mean, average-study effect; it is the model-averaged, bias-corrected effect for the reference-level combination directly, a study with Endog_FE = 0 and Reg_OECDEurope = 0. Each factor’s coefficient is the difference associated with switching that indicator to 1, and, unlike under the mean-difference coding used in earlier work on this dataset, can be compared directly against the corresponding CHE coefficient in Table 6. One should examine the sign, magnitude, and credibility interval of each moderator, particularly those with high PIPs in Panel B, in the same way the CHE coefficients in Table 6 are examined for statistical and substantive significance.

Panel D reports the residual heterogeneity (tau) and heterogeneity allocation (rho) that remain after conditioning on the retained moderators. A large tau relative to the intercept indicates that substantial unexplained variability in the true effect persists even after accounting for the moderators.

Note that rho here means something different from the rho in Section 4. In multi-level RoBMA, rho indicates the proportion of heterogeneity allocated to the cluster-level component: rho = 0 means all heterogeneity is within clusters, rho = 1 means all heterogeneity is between clusters, and rho = 0.5 means equal split.

Decision point. The moderator set entering this model is narrower than in earlier work on this dataset: Table 9’s BIC pre-selection currently retains only Endog_FE among the 18 candidate moderators. Reg_OECDEurope is carried into the model only because Table 11’s two best-practice scenarios require it, not because it clears the BIC screen.

Endog_FE is strongly corroborated across both methods, and the comparison is now direct rather than requiring a mean-difference subtraction. CHE finds it significant (coefficient −0.081, SE 0.028, p = 0.014; Table 6), and RoBMA assigns it strong support (PIP = 0.890, inclusion Bayes factor = 8.094), with an estimated effect of −0.079 (95% CrI [−0.148, 0.000], median −0.084) that closely matches the CHE coefficient in both sign and magnitude. Reg_OECDEurope, consistent with its BIC performance, receives little support (PIP = 0.200, inclusion Bayes factor = 0.251) and should be read as a scenario-construction device for Table 11 rather than as a substantive finding.

This specification is deliberately narrow, and excludes two of the three moderators Table 6 finds significant under CHE – LaggedDV and Endog_IV – because the current BIC screen does not retain them. Readers should treat the RoBMA moderator results in Table 10 as conditional on this particular, BIC-motivated specification, not as the only reasonable one. Appendix C reports a robustness check that instead carries forward all three of CHE’s significant moderators (Endog_FE, Endog_IV, LaggedDV) alongside Reg_OECDEurope, refit under the same treatment-coding/pooled_effect() convention used here. Reassuringly, that alternative specification finds the same decisive evidence for an overall Effect component (inclusion Bayes factor exceeding 119,999, versus more than 59,999 here) and an average-study bias-corrected mean (0.123, 95% CrI [0.075, 0.172]) nearly identical to this specification’s own (0.122, [0.073, 0.171]; see Appendix C).

9.7 Best-Practice Predictions

Table 11 is the RoBMA counterpart to Table 7 and should be read alongside it. It asks the same question: what effect size would we expect from a methodologically rigorous study? But it answers that question using the publication-bias-corrected coefficients from Table 10 rather than the FAT-PET-corrected coefficients from Table 6. The best-practice covariate values match those used in Table 7 for the one moderator the two models now share, so differences between the two sets of predictions are only partly attributable to the difference in the publication bias correction. A substantial part is attributable to specification: the RoBMA model conditions on a much smaller moderator set than Table 7’s nineteen regressors – just Endog_FE, the single moderator currently retained by Table 9’s BIC pre-selection, plus one regional dummy rather than all four (see the Best-practice scenarios subsection below) – so the two predictions should be read as broadly comparable rather than strictly like-for-like (see the Decision point following Table 10).

9.7.1 Two types of intervals

Table 11 reports two types of interval for each best-practice scenario. The credibility interval for the mean captures uncertainty about the model-averaged mean effect at the specified covariate values. This is the RoBMA analogue of the confidence interval in Table 7: it reflects estimation uncertainty only, not variability across future studies, and narrows as the number of studies increases. The prediction interval for the true effect is wider because it also incorporates residual effect heterogeneity: even among studies that exactly match the best-practice profile, true effects will vary due to factors not captured by the model. This is the RoBMA analogue of the prediction interval in Table 7. Both intervals are reported on the Fisher’s z scale and converted to partial correlation coefficients via the inverse transformation \(\text{PCC} = \tanh(z)\).

9.7.2 Best-practice scenarios

The two scenarios follow Table 7’s covariate values exactly, though the moderator set now consists only of Endog_FE and Reg_OECDEurope. Scenario BP#1 represents a non-OECD/Europe study using fixed effects for endogeneity (Endog_FE = 1), with Reg_OECDEurope set to zero. Scenario BP#2 does the same for an OECD/Europe study. Table 11 presents these two scenarios as Panel A (non-OECD/Europe) and Panel B (OECD/Europe), matching Table 7’s panel structure; the complete list of covariate values each panel is evaluated at is reported in a note below each panel. Because the current specification retains only Endog_FE and Reg_OECDEurope, out of Table 7’s nineteen regressors, the two RoBMA scenarios are narrower than their Table 7 counterparts, not fully parallel to them.

Another difference is that Reg_OECDEurope is the only regional dummy carried in this model, rather than all four used in Table 7 (Reg_OECDEurope, Reg_US, Reg_Africa, and Reg_Asia). An earlier estimation that included all four encountered convergence problems, which can arise when a RoBMA model includes categorical moderators with sparse cells – some regions here were represented by as few as four studies. Because neither best-practice scenario distinguishes among the non-OECD/Europe regions, the remaining three (Reg_US, Reg_Africa, and Reg_Asia) were folded into a single combined reference category alongside Reg_Other.

What to look for. The width of the prediction intervals reflects estimated residual heterogeneity. A very wide prediction interval relative to the credibility interval signals that substantial heterogeneity remains even after conditioning on all retained moderators, and the best-practice estimate should be interpreted as a central tendency rather than a precise forecast. The comparison of point estimates between Table 7 and Table 11 – and what their convergence or divergence implies – is taken up in Table 12 and the discussion in Section 10.

10 Comparing the Two Approaches

The two correction methods examined in this protocol – FAT-PET, applied in Sections 6 through 8, and RoBMA, applied in Section 9 – rest on different assumptions about the selection process. This section draws together the key results and explains how a reader should weigh the two sets of estimates.

10.1 The core comparison

Starting at the top of Table 12, the uncorrected CHE mean effect of 0.175 (95% CI [0.139, 0.212]) is reduced by roughly 76 percent under the FAT-PET correction, to a mean effect indistinguishable from zero (0.042, 95% CI [-0.025, 0.108]), and by roughly 30 percent under the RoBMA correction, to a mean effect of 0.122 (95% CrI [0.073, 0.171]). At the unconditional level the two methods now reach genuinely different conclusions, not just a difference in classification: FAT-PET’s correction leaves an effect that cannot be distinguished from zero, while RoBMA’s correction leaves a small effect whose 95% credible interval excludes zero entirely. The gap between the two point estimates, 0.080 in Fisher’s z, exceeds the Doucouliagos (2011) benchmark for a small effect used elsewhere in this protocol, and neither estimate falls inside the other’s interval.

The RoBMA unconditional estimate is corroborated by Table 8’s independent, moderator-free intercept-only estimate (0.121, CrI [0.073, 0.170]), which the pooled estimate above closely tracks – a reassuring cross-check, since the two come from entirely separate model fits.

As noted previously, RoBMA’s inclusion Bayes factor for the Effect component in this model (exceeding 59,999) is, strictly, a test of the reference-level intercept under treatment coding – the estimate for a study with Endog_FE = 0 and Reg_OECDEurope = 0 – rather than a direct test of the pooled effect reported above (see Model specification in Section 9.6). The moderator-free test of whether an overall effect exists at all is Table 8’s intercept-only model, which independently finds decisive evidence for one (inclusion Bayes factor exceeding 59,999) and agrees with the pooled estimate above.

10.1.1 Run the script

Code 
source("Protocol_Table12.R")

10.1.2 Display the output

Code 
read_excel("Table12_ComparisonSummary.xlsx") |> knitr::kable(align = "llrlll")
knitr::asis_output(paste0(
  '<div style="margin-top: 0.25em; text-align: left;"><p><em>Note: All estimates are on the ',
  'Fisher\'s z scale. Partial correlation (PCC) values are omitted here since tanh() is nearly ',
  'the identity function near zero, so the PCC values are almost identical to those shown. Every ',
  'row reports a 95% interval for the mean rather than a standard error or a prediction interval, ',
  'so that interval width is directly comparable across rows; prediction intervals for the true ',
  'effect remain available in Table 7 and Table 11. The FAT-PET rows report a genuine ',
  'confidence interval (frequentist, built from the same Satterthwaite degrees of freedom used ',
  'throughout this protocol), while the RoBMA rows report a credible interval: RoBMA is a Bayesian ',
  'method, so its interval summarizes the posterior distribution rather than repeated-sampling ',
  'coverage.</em></p></div>\n\n'
))

Under the FAT-PET correction, the predicted effect for a best-practice study is small and slightly negative for both scenarios (-0.022 for non-OECD/Europe, -0.043 for OECD/Europe). Under the RoBMA correction, the best-practice predicted effect is small and positive for both scenarios (0.053 and 0.046 respectively). This amounts to a gap of roughly 0.075 (non-OECD/Europe) and 0.089 (OECD/Europe) in Fisher’s z, above the Doucouliagos (2011) small-effect benchmark in both scenarios.

Unlike at the unconditional level, every one of these four best-practice point estimates has a confidence or credible interval that includes zero, so neither method finds a best-practice effect that is statistically distinguishable from zero, even though the RoBMA figures sit consistently above the FAT-PET ones. This produces a genuine asymmetry worth noting: RoBMA’s unconditional estimate is the one quantity in this comparison whose interval excludes zero, but conditioning on the best-practice covariate profile widens that interval enough to include zero again. Part of the remaining FAT-PET/RoBMA gap at the best-practice level may reflect genuine differences between the two corrections at a specific covariate profile, and part may reflect the fact that the RoBMA meta-regression conditions on a much smaller and different moderator set than the FAT-PET regressions.

Appendix C tests this directly, refitting the RoBMA meta-regression with an alternative, CHE-motivated moderator set under the same treatment-coding/pooled_effect() convention used in the primary specification. The resulting best-practice predictions (0.038 and 0.029, versus 0.053 and 0.046 here) sit closer to zero but on the same side of it, and the model finds the same decisive evidence for an overall effect (inclusion Bayes factor exceeding 119,999, versus more than 59,999 here) – confirming that the asymmetry just described (a nonzero unconditional estimate whose interval closes up around zero once best-practice covariates are conditioned on) holds regardless of which of the two moderator sets is used, even though the exact best-practice point estimates shift somewhat with the choice of moderators.

10.2 Why the two methods diverge

FAT-PET and RoBMA embed different models of the selection process, and that structural difference is real regardless of what any one dataset happens to show. As explained at the start of Section 9, FAT-PET assumes the probability of publication is a monotone function of the standard error; when selection instead operates on the sign of the effect or at discrete significance thresholds, the linear correction can in principle overshoot, driving estimates too far toward zero. The z-plot in Figure 3 shows two distinct spikes in the empirical distribution of z-statistics – one at z = 0 and one at z ≈ 1.96 – consistent with selection on both sign and significance, a pattern a linear standard-error correction cannot represent. This diagnosis does not rest on RoBMA alone: the PML step-function models in Section 6’s robustness checks, an entirely separate frequentist method, found the same sign-based asymmetry (\(\hat{\lambda}_2 = 0.27\), with a bootstrap confidence interval excluding 1), so two independent approaches agree the selection process has a feature FAT-PET’s smooth, standard-error-only correction cannot represent. This mechanism now has a larger empirical gap to explain than in earlier versions of this comparison (see The core comparison above), which makes the divergence a genuine empirical finding at the unconditional level rather than a narrow, threshold-sensitive distinction.

10.3 Overall conclusion

Three conclusions follow. First, publication bias in this literature is severe, and every method examined here agrees on that point (inclusion Bayes factors for the Publication Bias component exceed 59,999 in every RoBMA specification fitted, and the FAT-PET-corrected mean sits far below the raw CHE mean).

Second, unlike in earlier work on this dataset, FAT-PET and RoBMA no longer agree at the unconditional level. FAT-PET’s correction leaves an effect statistically indistinguishable from zero (0.042, 95% CI [-0.025, 0.108]); RoBMA’s correction leaves a small positive effect whose 95% credible interval excludes zero (0.122, [0.073, 0.171]), a figure that closely tracks the independent, moderator-free estimate from the intercept-only model in Table 8 (0.121, [0.073, 0.170]). This is a genuine divergence between the two frameworks at this level, not merely a difference in how close each one’s classification threshold sits to a shared estimate.

Third, at the best-practice level the two methods part ways on sign – FAT-PET’s corrected estimates are small and negative, RoBMA’s are small and positive – but every one of the four best-practice intervals, both methods and both scenarios, includes zero, so neither method finds a best-practice effect distinguishable from zero. RoBMA’s own verdict is stable across specification: Appendix C’s CHE-motivated alternative moderator set finds the same decisive evidence for an overall effect and an almost identical average-study estimate (0.123 versus 0.122).

The honest summary for a reader is that the unadjusted literature substantially overstates the effect of social capital on economic growth, that publication bias is severe under any correction method considered here, and that whether a nonzero effect survives correction depends on which method is used. Under RoBMA, a small positive effect survives at the unconditional level, and does so consistently across both moderator sets tested (the primary specification and Appendix C’s alternative); under FAT-PET, it does not. At the best-practice level, no specification examined here, under either method, finds an effect distinguishable from zero.

No single point estimate in this protocol should be read as the definitive answer, and the FAT-PET/RoBMA divergence at the unconditional level is itself among the protocol’s central methodological findings: two defensible approaches to correcting the same data for publication bias can disagree about whether an effect exists at all, even as they agree closely once the estimate is conditioned on a specific covariate profile.

12 Appendix A: Sensitivity to the Choice of Rho

Because \(\rho\) is assumed rather than estimated (Section 4), it is good practice to verify that the conclusions of the analysis do not depend on the particular value chosen. The logic is the same as for any robustness check around an unidentified assumption: re-estimate the key quantities across the full range of values the assumption could plausibly take, and ask whether the conclusions that matter remain stable. If they do, the assumption is not driving the results and the main-text value can be reported with confidence. If they do not, the dependence must be disclosed and the range of possible conclusions reported alongside the point estimate.

The check re-fits the intercept-only CHE model across a grid of \(\rho\) from 0 to 0.95, holding everything else fixed, and records the mean effect (the CHE intercept), its cluster-robust standard error, and the two variance components. A value of \(\rho = 0\) corresponds to the hierarchical-effects model, in which a study’s estimates share only a common study-level random effect and their sampling errors are treated as uncorrelated; values approaching 1 assume that a study’s estimates share almost all of their sampling error. The grid is deliberately wider than the values most applications would consider plausible, so that the display is conservative.

12.1 Run the script

Code 
# Note: this script takes approximately 6 minutes to run.
source("Protocol_RhoSensitivity.R")

12.2 Display the output

Code 
library(knitr)

include_graphics("Figure_RhoIntercept.png")
Code 
include_graphics("Figure_RhoVarianceComponents.png")

What to look for. In the running example, the mean effect is stable across this range. The CHE intercept declines gradually and monotonically from 0.194 at \(\rho = 0\) to 0.161 at \(\rho = 0.95\), a movement that is small relative to the standard error of the estimate, which itself stays close to 0.018 to 0.019 throughout. Every value in this range is well away from zero and of similar magnitude, so no conclusion about the sign, significance, or approximate size of the mean effect turns on the choice of \(\rho\). The variance components shift more visibly, and in opposite directions: between-study heterogeneity (\(\hat{\tau}\)) falls from 0.154 to 0.109 while within-study heterogeneity (\(\hat{\omega}\)) rises from 0.147 to 0.174. This reallocation is mechanical: as \(\rho\) increases, more of the observed similarity among a study’s estimates is attributed to correlated sampling error and correspondingly less to a shared study-level true effect. Both components remain substantively important at every value of \(\rho\), so the qualitative picture is also unchanged.

The stability of the standard error is not incidental. The cluster-robust (CR2) standard errors used throughout this protocol are designed to remain valid even when the working model for the dependence structure is misspecified (Pustejovsky and Tipton, 2022), and choosing the wrong \(\rho\) is one such misspecification. The robust standard errors thus provide a first line of protection against a poorly chosen \(\rho\), and the sensitivity analysis confirms that the point estimate is stable as well. Together they make the analysis robust to the fact that \(\rho\) cannot be identified from the data.

For write-up purposes, it is usually enough to report the value of \(\rho\) used, state that a sensitivity analysis was conducted over the full plausible range, and summarize the result in a sentence or two. The full numeric grid remains available in Table_RhoSensitivity.xlsx. Where a check of this kind reveals that a conclusion flips within the plausible range of \(\rho\), that finding should be reported prominently rather than buried: it means the analysis is genuinely sensitive to an unidentified assumption, and readers need to know the range of estimates the data are consistent with.

13 Appendix B: Outlier and Influence Analysis

Any meta-analysis that includes a large number of effect sizes may be sensitive to a small number of highly influential observations or studies. This appendix presents two complementary analyses: observation-level influence diagnostics and a study-level jackknife.

13.1 Observation-Level Influence Diagnostics

The first analysis uses the influence() function from metafor, which is available for models estimated by rma() (the univariate random-effects model) but not for rma.mv(). A standard RE model is therefore fitted to all 957 observations for the purpose of these diagnostics only. The resulting plot displays a suite of influence statistics for each observation, including studentized residuals, Cook’s distances, hat values (leverage), and changes in the estimated \(\hat{\tau}^2\) and the overall mean when each observation is dropped. Observations with an absolute studentized residual greater than three are flagged.

13.2 Study-Level Jackknife

The second analysis is a study-level jackknife on the preferred CHE model. Each of the 83 studies is dropped from the dataset in turn, the CHE intercept-only model is refitted on the remaining 82 studies, and the resulting intercept is recorded. The jackknife estimates are displayed as a forest-plot-style figure, sorted by the magnitude of the leave-one-out intercept. The accompanying table ranks the 83 studies by the absolute change in the intercept when they are excluded, identifying the studies that have the greatest influence on the overall mean estimate.

This analysis is computationally expensive: fitting 83 CHE models in sequence takes approximately two hours. It is recommended to run this script overnight or in a background session.

13.3 Run the script

Code 
# Note: this script takes approximately 2 hours to run (83 CHE model fits).
# Recommended to run overnight or in a background session.
source("Protocol_Outliers.R")

What to look for. In the influence diagnostics, observations with very large studentized residuals represent effect sizes that are far from the model’s predictions and may reflect coding errors, unusual sample characteristics, or highly heterogeneous studies. In the jackknife, studies that cause a large change in the CHE intercept when dropped are disproportionately influential. If a small number of studies drive the overall estimate, the robustness of conclusions depends on those studies’ reliability and representativeness.

Decision point. In this dataset, the diagnostics point to a small number of specific studies rather than a diffuse problem. One observation from Pan and He is the clear standout across every influence statistic at once (studentized residual ≈ 8.7, Cook’s distance ≈ 0.35, both far above anything else in the sample): it is one of sixteen effect sizes this study reports, several of which are exact or near-exact duplicates of one another, and its own value (partial correlation ≈ 0.45) is well above the rest of the study’s range (roughly 0.13 to 0.37). Two single-observation studies are also flagged: Kaldaru and Parts (partial correlation 0.92) and Holthe (two observations, one at 0.96), both reporting far larger effects than is typical elsewhere in the literature. The jackknife results confirm the same picture from a different angle: dropping Kaldaru and Parts changes the CHE intercept the most (-0.0098), followed by Holthe (-0.0090) and Algan and Cahuc, a 33-observation study whose own average effect is unusually high (-0.0082). Lyon, the single largest study in the sample at 68 observations, is also flagged, but for the opposite reason: dropping it increases the intercept (+0.0062), meaning its many observations pull the pooled mean down rather than up.

Even so, the overall picture is reassuring. Across all 83 studies, the leave-one-out intercept never moves outside roughly 0.165 to 0.181, a narrow band around the full-sample estimate of 0.175, and no single study is capable of overturning the qualitative conclusion that the raw, uncorrected literature reports a positive average association. The practical recommendation is to verify that Kaldaru and Parts, Holthe, and Pan and He are coded correctly, since partial correlations above roughly 0.9 are rare enough in this literature to warrant a second look at the original source – but not to exclude them without that check, since the jackknife shows the overall conclusion does not depend on any one of them.

14 Appendix C: RoBMA Meta-Regression with an Alternative Moderator Set (Robustness Check)

Section 9.6’s Decision point flags that the RoBMA meta-regression in Table 10 conditions on a narrow moderator set (Endog_FE and Reg_OECDEurope) chosen by an automated BIC pre-selection step. That set excludes two of the three moderators the CHE meta-regression finds significant (Table 6): LaggedDV and Endog_IV. This appendix reports a robustness check that instead retains all three of CHE’s significant moderators – Endog_FE, Endog_IV, and LaggedDV – alongside Reg_OECDEurope, again included only because the best-practice scenarios below require it. The question this check answers is narrow but consequential: does RoBMA’s headline verdict about whether an overall effect exists depend on which moderators happen to survive the BIC screen?

This is a robustness check, not a replacement for the protocol’s primary RoBMA specification. Its results are summarized in Section 9.6’s Decision point and in Section 10; this appendix provides the full detail behind those summaries.

14.1 Model specification

The model is fit the same way as the primary specification in Table 10: measure = “ZCOR”, clustered on newid, binary moderators declared as factors (so RoBMA applies the categorical-moderator prior rather than treating a 0/1 indicator as continuous), treatment (dummy) contrasts, and the average-study bias-corrected mean computed via pooled_effect() rather than marginal_means() – the same convention described in Section 9.6’s Model specification. This model was originally fit under RoBMA’s default mean-difference (meandif) contrasts with marginal_means(), before that convention was corrected for the primary specification following correspondence with RoBMA’s developer. It has since been refit under the current convention, so the comparison reported below isolates the effect of moderator-set choice: both this model and Table 10 now differ only in which moderators are included, not in how the results are computed.

A first attempt at this fit, using the same MCMC settings as Table 10, failed to converge: the intercept (R-hat 1.051, ESS 238) and LaggedDV (R-hat 1.080, ESS 90) both fell short of the protocol’s convergence bar (R-hat < 1.05, ESS ≥ 500; see Section 9.3), with Reg_OECDEurope’s ESS (339) also falling short. Because the intercept is the parameter the Effect-component Bayes factor is computed from, this meant the headline finding from that first attempt could not be trusted. The sampling budget was doubled (sample 20000 → 40000, burnin 10000 → 20000, adapt 10000 → 20000) and the model refit from scratch; that doubled budget was retained for the later treatment-coding refit as well. The results reported below are from that final, doubled-budget, treatment-coded fit.

# Protocol_Table10_FYI.R fits the meta-regression; Protocol_Table11_FYI.R
# derives the best-practice predictions from the saved model object (well
# under two minutes, since it only calls predict() on the saved fit).
source("Protocol_Table10_FYI.R")
source("Protocol_Table11_FYI.R")

These predictions are derived from the four-moderator RoBMA meta-regression in Protocol_Table10_FYI.R (Endog_FE, Endog_IV, LaggedDV, Reg_OECDEurope -- the three moderators Table 6 Panel B classifies as "Evidence of Moderator Effect," plus Reg_OECDEurope for this regional comparison), rather than the protocol's primary BIC-selected two-moderator model (Table 10 / Table 11). Predictions are evaluated at Endog_FE = 1, Endog_IV = 1, LaggedDV = 0, Reg_OECDEurope = 1 (the reference category -- combining Reg_US, Reg_Africa, Reg_Asia, and Reg_Other -- is implied when Reg_OECDEurope = 0). se(z) and publication year are not covariates in this model: RoBMA corrects for publication bias internally rather than through a linear se(z) term, and publication year was not retained by the BIC pre-selection in Table 9.

What to look for. Panel A shows the same decisive evidence for all three components as the primary specification: Effect, Heterogeneity, and Publication Bias each exceed an inclusion Bayes factor of 119,999 (posterior probability 1.000). As in Table 10, this Effect Bayes factor is a property of the treatment-coded reference-level intercept (Endog_FE = 0, Endog_IV = 0, LaggedDV = 0, Reg_OECDEurope = 0), not a direct test of the pooled effect (see Section 9.6’s Model specification). The pooled, average-study bias-corrected mean, from pooled_effect(), is 0.123, 95% CrI [0.075, 0.172] – nearly identical to the primary specification’s 0.122, [0.073, 0.171], and to the independent, moderator-free intercept-only estimate in Table 8 (0.121, [0.073, 0.170]). This three-way agreement, across a BIC-selected two-moderator model, a CHE-motivated four-moderator model, and a model with no moderators at all, is the clearest evidence in this protocol that the corrected pooled_effect() convention is doing the right thing.

Panel B shows a mixed picture across the four moderators, and one that differs from the picture reported under the earlier, superseded mean-difference fit. Endog_FE remains strongly supported (PIP = 0.931, inclusion Bayes factor = 13.502), with an estimated effect of −0.090 (95% CrI [−0.157, 0.000], median −0.093) that closely matches the CHE coefficient in Table 6 (−0.081, p = 0.014) – corroborated in both specifications, under both contrast conventions. LaggedDV’s support, by contrast, weakens under the corrected convention: its posterior inclusion probability falls from 0.725 under the earlier mean-difference fit to 0.482 here, now below one-half, with an attenuated coefficient (−0.042, 95% CrI [−0.166, 0.000], median 0.000) well short of the CHE coefficient it once appeared to corroborate (−0.058, p = 0.046). Endog_IV remains weakly supported either way (PIP = 0.291, inclusion Bayes factor = 0.411; coefficient −0.013, 95% CrI [−0.082, 0.000], median 0.000), despite being significant under CHE (−0.039, p = 0.045) – the one CHE-significant moderator RoBMA does not corroborate in either specification, which looks like a genuine divergence between the two frameworks rather than a computational artifact, since it persists under the corrected convention. Reg_OECDEurope remains weakly supported (PIP = 0.222), consistent with its role as a scenario-construction device rather than a substantive finding.

The best-practice predictions in Panels A and B of the table above (0.038 and 0.029 in Fisher’s z, for non-OECD/Europe and OECD/Europe respectively) sit closer to zero than the primary specification’s corresponding predictions (0.053 and 0.046; Table 11), but on the same, positive side of it, with credibility and prediction intervals that comfortably include zero under both specifications. This is the same asymmetry described in Section 10: the unconditional estimate’s interval excludes zero, but conditioning on the best-practice covariate profile widens the interval enough to include zero again, and that pattern now holds under both moderator sets tested, not just the primary one.

Decision point. Taken together, this robustness check answers the question posed at the start of this appendix, and the answer is reassuring rather than concerning: RoBMA’s headline conclusion that an overall effect exists does not depend on which of these two moderator sets is used. Both the BIC-motivated two-moderator specification and the CHE-motivated four-moderator specification find decisive evidence for an effect (inclusion Bayes factor exceeding 59,999 in the primary specification, exceeding 119,999 here) and an almost identical average-study bias-corrected mean (0.122 versus 0.123). An earlier version of this check, run before the treatment-coding correction described in Section 9.6’s Model specification was applied, had instead found only weak evidence against an overall effect (inclusion Bayes factor 0.441) and a noticeably smaller average-study mean (0.023) – a genuine-looking specification-sensitivity finding that did not survive being recomputed under the corrected convention, and is best read as a caution about how easily a computational artifact can masquerade as a substantive result. The one real difference between the two specifications is at the level of individual moderators: LaggedDV’s apparent corroboration of CHE weakens substantially under the corrected convention (posterior inclusion probability falls from 0.725 to 0.482), while Endog_FE remains robustly corroborated and Endog_IV remains weakly supported by RoBMA despite CHE significance under both specifications. At the best-practice level, both specifications also agree that no prediction is statistically distinguishable from zero, though the CHE-motivated specification’s point estimates sit somewhat closer to zero than the primary specification’s. Readers should take from this appendix that the protocol’s central conclusions – an overall effect that survives at the unconditional level but not once conditioned on best-practice covariates – are robust to the choice between these two defensible moderator sets, once both are computed under the same, correct convention. Convergence, reported in full above, is excellent throughout, resolving the marginal LaggedDV shortfall (ESS 492) that the earlier fit had disclosed.
